summary:
Marriage between same-sex couples became legal in Greece in February 2024 under Law 5089/2024, making it the first country with a majority Orthodox Christian population to enact marriage equality. The same law added sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics as equal-treatment grounds in goods and services, education, healthcare, housing and social protection. Civil unions have been available since 2015, adoption and foster care by same-sex couples are permitted, and the age of consent is 15 for everyone. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Greek law can have that relationship recognised in marriage.

Legal gender change has been available on a self-declaration basis since 2017. TGEU's Trans Rights Index and Map 2025 records Greece meeting 21 of its 32 indicators; the identified gaps include age restrictions on changes of forename, the absence of a national action plan on trans rights, and no legal recognition of trans or non-binary parenthood. Greece ranked seventh in Europe on the 2025 Rainbow Map.

Conversion practices are banned for minors and intersex genital mutilation was criminalised in 2022; the ban does not extend to adults. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity was prohibited in 2023. Discrimination and hate-speech protections are in force.

In March 2024 a mob of about 150 people attacked two trans people in Thessaloniki; 21 people were arrested, 11 of them minors, and a masked group then attacked counter-protesters. In July 2025 the Crete Court of Appeal convicted three French tourists for an attack carried out in 2017. The Orthodox Church officially opposed marriage equality, and transphobic comments were directed at Eurovision contestants.

In Koutra and Katzaki v. Greece (European Court of Human Rights, application 459/16, judgment 2017), the court examined the 2013 stopping and mistreatment of transgender sex workers and their lawyer in Athens, including street stops and removal from cars; the complaints against the officers were discontinued.

The EU Fundamental Rights Agency's LGBTIQ survey III, published in 2024, found that 63% of respondents in Greece avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner, against an EU-27 average of 53%; 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault, against 29% across the EU; and only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ, against 51% across the EU.

The European Court of Human Rights condemned Greece for detaining an LGBTI Iranian refugee pending deportation, finding a violation of Article 3. A criminal case was opened over an online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Foreign Office updated its Greece travel advice for LGBTQ+ holidaymakers in April 2024, noting that same-sex relations are legal, that civil unions have existed since 2015, that marriage has been available since February 2024, that the age of consent is 15 for all, and that legal gender change is possible; travellers were advised to remain alert.

Greece's Justice Ministry pledged a working group on the rights of cohabiting same-sex couples in 2008, feeding into forthcoming unmarried-couples legislation; civil unions followed in 2015 and marriage equality in February 2024.

TGEU reported in May 2025 that backsliding was outpacing progress across Europe for the first time; Greece's 21 of 32 indicators sit against that regional trend rather than apart from it.
localsOnly:
In December 2021 four trans detainees were ordered transferred to the women's prisons of Korydallou in Athens by decision of the General Secretary for Crime-Prevention Policy Sofia Nikolaou, after each had petitioned for transfer stating that they identify and wish to be treated as women. The four, three Greek and one Bulgarian, had been held at Trikala and Corfu prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender. It was the first documented transfer of trans prisoners to a women's facility in Greece; default placement had followed the male facilities, and an on-request transfer route to women's facilities existed.

28% of respondents in Greece to the 2024 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey felt discriminated against at work, against an EU average of 19%.
outOfScopeNotes:
No national action plan on trans rights exists, and trans or non-binary parenthood has no legal recognition; age restrictions continue to apply to changes of forename. These are standing gaps rather than pending measures.

The conversion-practices ban covers minors only; the sources do not establish what protection, if any, applies to adults.

Whether the March 2024 Thessaloniki arrests produced convictions is not sourced, and the outcome of the criminal case over the online incitement post is likewise not sourced.

Whether Greece has complied with the European Court of Human Rights judgment on the detained LGBTI refugee is not sourced, and no disciplinary outcome is recorded for the discontinued complaints in the Koutra and Katzaki case.
